title: Calcium imaging and genetically encoded indicators
text:
12_02  CALCIUM IMAGING AND GENETICALLY ENCODED INDICATORS

Optogenetics gave neuroscience a way to write to neurons with light. The complementary revolution was a way to read from them with light, not one or two cells at a time as with a glass electrode, but hundreds to many thousands of identified neurons at once, over days and weeks, in behaving animals. This section explains how that works, from the chemistry of fluorescent indicators to the signal processing used to turn movies of glowing cells into estimates of spikes. For an AI-minded reader, it is also the story of how neuroscience became a big-data field, with datasets large enough that machine learning stopped being optional.

WHY CALCIUM?

When a neuron fires an action potential, voltage-gated calcium channels in its membrane open briefly (Chapter 5), and calcium ions flow in. The free calcium concentration inside a resting neuron is very low, on the order of 50 to 100 nanomolar, while outside it is around 1 to 2 millimolar, a gradient of roughly ten thousand to one. A single spike therefore produces a sizeable relative rise in intracellular calcium, which then decays over tens to hundreds of milliseconds as pumps and buffers remove it. Calcium is thus a natural, if slow and blurred, proxy for spiking. It is also a second messenger in its own right: it triggers transmitter release, and calcium entry through NMDA receptors is the trigger for long-term potentiation (Chapter 7). Measuring calcium reports both electrical output and some of the chemistry of plasticity.

SYNTHETIC DYES

The first practical tools were synthetic fluorescent dyes, developed largely by Roger Tsien and colleagues in the 1980s. Tsien's insight was to build a molecule that combines a calcium-selective chelator, based on the structure of EGTA, with a fluorophore, so that binding calcium changes its fluorescence. Fura-2, described by Grynkiewicz, Poenie and Tsien in 1985, shifts its excitation spectrum when it binds calcium, which allows ratiometric measurement: dividing the fluorescence at two excitation wavelengths cancels out differences in dye concentration and cell thickness. Later dyes such as Oregon Green BAPTA were used for imaging neurons in tissue.

The relationship between fluorescence and calcium follows basic binding chemistry. For an indicator with dissociation constant K_d, the fraction bound is

  fraction bound = [Ca] / ([Ca] + K_d)

so fluorescence rises steeply when [Ca] is near K_d and saturates far above it. Many indicators bind cooperatively, which is better modelled with a Hill equation:

  fraction bound = [Ca]^n / ([Ca]^n + K_d^n)

with Hill coefficient n greater than 1. Cooperativity makes the response more switch-like, which helps detect single spikes but makes the signal nonlinear in the number of spikes. Keep that nonlinearity in mind; it matters when we try to infer spikes.

Dyes have a key limitation: they must be loaded into cells, by injection or by membrane-permeant forms, and they label cells indiscriminately and only for hours. They cannot follow the same neurons over weeks, and they cannot be targeted to a cell type.

GREEN FLUORESCENT PROTEIN AND GENETIC INDICATORS

The solution came from a jellyfish. Green fluorescent protein (GFP), from Aequorea victoria, was isolated by Osamu Shimomura. Martin Chalfie showed that it could be expressed as a genetic tag in other organisms, and Tsien's laboratory engineered many variants and colours. The three shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Because GFP is a protein, its gene can be delivered and expressed in chosen cells, using the same promoters, Cre lines and viral vectors described for optogenetics.

A genetically encoded calcium indicator (GECI) couples a fluorescent protein to a calcium-sensing domain. The most widely used family, GCaMP, was introduced by Junichi Nakai, Masamichi Ohkura and Keiji Imoto in 2001. Its design is elegant: GFP is circularly permuted, meaning its original ends are joined and new ends are created near the chromophore, and calmodulin (a calcium-binding protein) is attached at one end and a calmodulin-binding peptide (M13, from myosin light-chain kinase) at the other. When calcium binds calmodulin, calmodulin wraps around M13, which changes the environment of the chromophore and makes it much brighter.

Early GCaMPs were too dim and slow to see single spikes reliably in vivo. Over a decade of protein engineering, much of it at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus through its GENIE project, improved them through rounds of mutagenesis and screening. In 2013 Chen and colleagues reported GCaMP6 in Nature, with variants named by kinetics (6s for slow but sensitive, 6m medium, 6f fast) that could detect single action potentials in many cortical neurons in vivo. Later generations (jGCaMP7, jGCaMP8, the latter reported by Zhang and colleagues in Nature in 2023) pushed rise times faster, toward the timescale of individual spikes. This was a textbook engineering loop: define a figure of merit, build a high-throughput screen, mutate, select, iterate. It is directed evolution, and it resembles optimisation by search in a design space.

TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY

Indicators are only half the system; the other half is optics. Brain tissue scatters visible light strongly, so a conventional microscope sees a blur below the top few tens of micrometres. Two-photon excitation microscopy, demonstrated for biology by Winfried Denk, James Strickler and Watt Webb in 1990, solves this using a physical trick. A fluorophore that normally absorbs one photon of, say, 488 nm can instead absorb two photons of roughly twice the wavelength (around 920 nm) almost simultaneously. The probability of this depends on the square of the light intensity, so with a pulsed infrared laser focused through an objective, significant excitation occurs only at the focal spot. Out-of-focus light causes negligible fluorescence, so every emitted photon can be assigned to the point being scanned, even if it scatters on the way out. Infrared also penetrates tissue better.

The microscope scans this focal spot across the field using galvanometric or resonant mirrors, building an image pixel by pixel, typically at around 30 frames per second for a field of several hundred micrometres containing hundreds of neurons. Depth in mouse cortex is usually limited to the upper layers, roughly 500 to 800 micrometres, without special techniques; three-photon microscopy with longer wavelengths can go deeper.

Other optical approaches trade resolution for coverage:

Head-mounted miniature microscopes, developed by Ghosh, Schnitzer and colleagues (published in 2011), weigh a few grams and let a mouse move freely while a one-photon microscope images through an implanted lens, including in deep structures such as hippocampus.

Light-sheet microscopy illuminates a whole plane at once. In 2013 Ahrens, Keller and colleagues used it to image activity in nearly all neurons of the brain of a larval zebrafish, an animal small and transparent enough to allow it, at about one volume per 1.3 seconds.

Mesoscopes with large fields of view, and multiplane systems, now record from tens of thousands of neurons in mouse cortex simultaneously.

FROM MOVIES TO SPIKES: THE PROCESSING PIPELINE

Raw output is a video of shifting, noisy, overlapping glows. Turning it into data requires a pipeline that a mechatronics student will recognise as signal processing plus estimation.

1. Motion correction. The brain moves with heartbeat, breathing and the animal's movement. Frames are registered to a reference, by rigid shifts estimated with phase correlation (a Fourier-domain method) and then by piecewise non-rigid corrections.

2. Source extraction. Which pixels belong to which neuron? A popular approach models the movie as a matrix Y (pixels by time) approximately factorised as

  Y ~ A C + B + E

where A holds spatial footprints of neurons (pixels by neurons), C holds their activity traces (neurons by time), B is background (including out-of-focus "neuropil" fluorescence), and E is noise. A and C are constrained to be non-negative and spatially sparse. This is constrained non-negative matrix factorisation (CNMF), introduced by Pnevmatikakis, Paninski and colleagues and implemented in the CaImAn toolbox. Suite2p, from Pachitariu, Stringer and colleagues, uses a related approach optimised for speed on large datasets.

3. Normalisation. Fluorescence is usually expressed as delta F over F:

  dF/F = (F(t) - F0) / F0

where F0 is a baseline, often a running low percentile of the trace, after subtracting a scaled neuropil signal.

4. Spike inference (deconvolution). Calcium rises fast and decays slowly, so the observed trace is roughly the spike train convolved with a kernel. A simple generative model is first-order autoregressive:

  c(t) = gamma * c(t-1) + s(t)
  y(t) = alpha * c(t) + b + noise(t)

where s(t) is the number of spikes in time bin t (non-negative, usually sparse), c(t) is calcium concentration, gamma = exp(-dt / tau_decay) captures the decay, and y(t) is the observed fluorescence. Inferring s from y is a sparse deconvolution problem: find the non-negative, sparse s that explains y. Methods include the fast non-negative deconvolution of Vogelstein and colleagues and the OASIS algorithm of Friedrich, Zhou and Paninski. Supervised alternatives train neural networks on datasets where calcium and electrical spikes were recorded simultaneously; the spikefinder benchmark compared such methods in 2018. The honest summary is that spike inference from calcium is good at estimating firing rates over tens to hundreds of milliseconds and much weaker at exact spike times or counts in bursts, especially given the indicator nonlinearity noted above.

5. Cell classification and tracking across days, which is needed to follow the same neurons through learning.

VOLTAGE IMAGING

Calcium is an indirect, slow, and mostly spike-related signal; it misses subthreshold voltage changes and inhibition. Genetically encoded voltage indicators aim to report membrane potential directly, with millisecond response. Designs include fluorescent proteins attached to voltage-sensing domains (for example the ASAP family from Michael Lin's laboratory) and engineered microbial rhodopsins whose fluorescence depends on voltage (such as Archon, from Boyden's group). The challenge is signal: the membrane is a thin layer, so few indicator molecules sit in it, and spikes are brief, so few photons are collected per spike. Voltage imaging is improving but remains harder than calcium imaging at scale.

Other genetically encoded sensors report neurotransmitters. Sensors built from bacterial binding proteins or from G-protein-coupled receptors fused to circularly permuted fluorescent proteins detect glutamate (iGluSnFR), dopamine (dLight, GRAB-DA), acetylcholine, serotonin and others. These let researchers watch dopamine transients during learning, a direct look at the reward prediction error signals of Chapter 6.

WHAT LARGE-SCALE IMAGING HAS SHOWN

Population recordings changed several ideas. A few examples:

Mixed and distributed coding. Many neurons respond to combinations of task variables, and behavioural variables are often decodable from many areas at once.

Movement everywhere. In 2019 Stringer, Pachitariu and colleagues reported in Science that a large fraction of activity in mouse visual cortex, recorded from around ten thousand neurons, was related to the animal's spontaneous facial and body movements, not just visual stimuli. Musall, Churchland and colleagues reported similar widespread movement-related activity across dorsal cortex in the same year. This complicated the classic picture of sensory areas as pure feature detectors.

Representational drift. Studies tracking the same neurons over days found that the set of neurons representing a given stimulus or location can change gradually even when behaviour is stable, for example in hippocampal place cells imaged by Ziv, Schnitzer and colleagues in 2013. How a downstream reader copes with a drifting code is an active question.

Open data. The Allen Institute's Brain Observatory released standardised two-photon datasets from mouse visual cortex, with stimuli, behaviour and processed traces, freely downloadable. This resembles the role of ImageNet in computer vision: shared benchmarks that let many groups test models on the same data.

CONNECTIONS TO AI AND MACHINE LEARNING

1. Neuroscience as a data science. A single imaging session can produce hundreds of gigabytes. Motion correction, source extraction and spike inference are machine learning problems: matrix factorisation, sparse coding, deconvolution, and increasingly deep networks trained on ground-truth data. Some segmentation tools use convolutional networks, the architecture whose biological roots were described in Chapter 8. There is a loop here: CNNs inspired partly by visual cortex are used to analyse recordings of visual cortex.

2. Matrix factorisation as a shared idea. The CNMF model Y ~ A C is the same mathematical family as non-negative matrix factorisation, used in machine learning for topic models and parts-based representations (Lee and Seung, 1999), and close to sparse dictionary learning, which Olshausen and Field used in 1996 to show that sparse codes for natural images produce receptive fields like V1 simple cells. Learning the "parts" of a signal under non-negativity and sparsity constraints appears in both brains and algorithms.

3. Dimensionality reduction and latent dynamics. With thousands of simultaneously recorded neurons, researchers ask whether activity lives on a low-dimensional manifold. Tools range from principal component analysis to latent variable models trained with deep learning, such as LFADS (latent factor analysis via dynamical systems, from Pandarinath, Sussillo and colleagues), which fits a recurrent neural network as a generative model of population activity. Models trained on many recordings, sometimes described as foundation models for neural data, are being explored. The same intuition, that high-dimensional observations are generated by a smaller latent state, underlies autoencoders and state-space models in ML.

4. Comparing representations. When one has population responses from a brain area and activations from a layer of a deep network for the same stimuli, they can be compared with methods such as representational similarity analysis or linear regression from model features to neural responses. Large imaging datasets made such model-brain comparisons statistically meaningful.

5. Drift and robustness. Representational drift raises a question familiar to anyone who deploys models: if the features change, how does the readout remain accurate? Proposed answers include the readout continually adapting, or drift occurring mainly in directions the readout ignores (a null space). Both ideas have analogues in ML, in continual learning (Chapter 11) and in the observation that networks can change many weights without changing their function.

SUMMARY

Calcium imaging converts spikes into light through calcium influx and engineered indicators, from Tsien's dyes to the GCaMP family; two-photon and other microscopes collect that light from many cells at once; and a signal processing pipeline of registration, matrix factorisation and deconvolution converts movies into estimated activity. The result made neuroscience a field of large datasets, recorded from identified cells over time, and tightly bound it to the same mathematics used in machine learning.
